title: Copy suppression
description: An attention head lowers predictions of tokens already present in context.

claims.heading: GPT-2 small’s attention head L10H7 mainly suppresses predicted tokens already present in context
Attention targeting (QK) and output writing (OV) explain much of GPT-2 small’s copy suppression
Copy suppression may improve calibration by reducing overconfidence in copied tokens
Copy suppression partly compensates when earlier token-copying heads are ablated
Negative heads across tasks and models share the same copy-suppression role
Does self-repair mainly come from mechanisms other than copy suppression?

related_findings.title: Compensation varies across models and training data
related_findings.summary: Later layers can partly make up for removed language-model components. This compensation varies with training data and model, and is weak in the tested tabular foundation models.

examples.headline: Later layers partly make up for removed attention layers in Chinchilla 7B.
Hierarchical training data strengthens toy models' compensation between heads; the layer-level difference loses significance after correction.
Layer ablations reveal little repair and more redundancy in the tested tabular foundation models.

related_findings.title: Suppressive heads across models and tasks
related_findings.summary: Groups of attention heads suppress copied tokens, labels supplied in context and answers to rules across several model families. These findings do not establish that the heads share the mechanism of copy-suppression head L10H7.

examples.headline: Selected heads jointly suppress in-context labels in Qwen3 and Llama; individual Llama heads have small effects.
Removing Pythia's output-cancelling heads improves rule-following accuracy; suppression depends on values read from attended tokens.
Removing distinct head groups raises copied-token scores before softmax in Llama2-7B-chat, OPT-6.7B and Baichuan-13B-chat.

related_findings.title: Other sources of compensation
related_findings.summary: Compensation can arise when softmax shifts attention weights between sources, or from heads that already counteract other components. Rescaling by the final normalization layer had a small effect in the tested instruction-tuned models, while rankings of interactions on indirect object identification (IOI) tasks do not establish how much each mechanism contributes.

examples.headline: GPT-2 Small heads already counteract others; final-normalization rescaling contributes little in tested instruction-tuned models.
Indirect object identification: copying heads interact more with suppressing than backup heads; compensation shares remain unquantified.
Softmax redistributes attention weights, making joint removal of similar sources more disruptive than either removal alone.

related_findings.title: Training changes suppressive roles
related_findings.summary: Suppressive roles can move between heads during pretraining and change during task fine-tuning. In Qwen3, adding up selected heads' separately measured effects suggests stronger suppression after instruction tuning.

examples.headline: Summing selected single-head effects shows stronger suppression of word meanings in Qwen3-4B instruct versus base model.
Unmodified indirect object identification fine-tuning strengthens heads suppressing correct names; Subject Duplication (repeated subjects) redirects suppression.
Pythia-160m's copy-suppression roles move between heads during training while indirect object identification metrics remain stable.

related_findings.title: Stored facts compete with contextual copies
related_findings.summary: In GPT-2 and Pythia, boosting suppressive heads can shift outputs toward factual answers, with GPT-2's gains depending strongly on whether the prompt supplies the fact. The heads' role in hallucination during retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) remains speculative.

examples.headline: Boosting suppressive attention increases factual wins in GPT-2 and Pythia on redefinition prompts.
Boosting GPT-2 heads yields more factual answers when the prompt's subject text contains the fact.
During hallucination, attention often targets correct text; copy suppression's role in causing hallucination remains speculative.

related_findings.title: Semantic variants and interacting suppressive heads
related_findings.summary: Copy suppression can target variants with related meanings, and suppressive heads can depend on each other. Toy sorting models can have similar circuits for producing copying and suppression outputs but differ in how their queries and keys determine attention.

examples.headline: GPT-2 Small's L10.h7 mediates L11.h10's curved response to the name-mover core.
Toy sorting heads resemble copy suppression in output (OV) circuits, but choose attention targets (QK) differently.
Copy suppression targets variants with related meanings beyond predictions from the cosine similarity of embeddings.

related_findings.title: MLP suppression depends on upstream attention
related_findings.summary: MLPs can suppress tokens promoted by earlier attention and strengthen attention's suppression of previous answers. Removing that attention weakens both effects.

examples.headline: Late token-erasing MLPs provide most later compensation; removing earlier attention weakens their suppression of promoted tokens.
Removing attention to previous answers weakens MLP suppression of those answers.

related_findings.title: A head's contribution depends on how it is measured
related_findings.summary: A head's apparent contribution can depend on the task, readout and intervention. Its direct contribution to token scores before softmax (direct logit attribution) can be negative while its score from replacing activations (patching) is positive, and heads that cancel other heads' outputs can support antonym answers.

examples.headline: Fair Lending task: GPT-2 Small head 10.7 has negative direct output contributions but positive activation-replacement scores.
Pythia canceller heads support antonym answers while remaining suppressive on country-capital prompts.

reading_list.why: Introduces copy suppression, causal tests and quantitative GPT-2 small analysis, including compensation after ablation on indirect object identification (IOI).
Tests copying and suppressing heads’ interactions independently in GPT-2 small IOI, using controlled ablations of head groups and confidence intervals.
Tests whether boosting suppressive heads retrieves stored facts or relies on facts already present in context.

known_gaps.summary: Open questions are whether models share the same mechanism, how much compensation after ablation it explains, when heads recall stored facts, whether confidence better matches accuracy, what individual heads do and how results depend on the intervention.
items: Suppressive heads appear across model families, but these studies do not establish L10H7’s full mechanism: how its query–key circuit directs attention and how it changes the output. Partial GPT-2 Medium tests and Pythia analyses leave unresolved how much of a head’s effect this mechanism explains beyond GPT-2 small.

Outside indirect object identification (IOI), the share of compensation after ablation (“self-repair”) due to copy suppression remains uncertain. Rankings of interactions between groups do not measure compensation shares, and other sources include components that already oppose the ablated component and redistribution of probabilities by softmax.

It remains unclear when boosting these heads retrieves stored facts rather than relies on contextual copies. The GPT-2 studies use different prompts, and factual output drops when the context lacks a factual hint.

The claim that copy suppression reduces overconfidence rests on limited language-model evidence. The original paper's figure caption and ablation description disagree about the intervention's direction.

Changing multiple heads together does not establish each head’s role, and in Pythia, specialization has not been established separately for heads L17H28 and L21H8. Direct attribution, which estimates a head’s output contribution, and output patching, which replaces its output, can also assign different signs to the same head’s effect.
It remains unresolved whether compensation after ablation (“self-repair”) measured by fully removing a component reflects the same behavior as gradually replacing its output (“graded swaps”).

The Qwen3 comparison of prediction suppression (“braking”) in base and instruction-tuned models adds up the effects of selected heads tested one at a time. It does not establish the effect of ablating those heads together.
